lawyer:
Nazmul Huda with Sigma Huda ------ For the Appellant 
Muhammadullah with Miah A. Gafur and, Shahabuddin Ahmed ------ for the Respondent
parties:
Mrs. Nilufar Majid
Vs.
Mokbol Ahmed
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal preferred u/s 47 of the Guardians and Wards Act), 1890; hereinafter referred to as the said Act, is directed against the judgment and Order dated 23-6-83 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Act VIII Case No. 452 of 1983 u/s 25 of the said Act dismissing the application of the petitioner-appellant for appointing herself as the guardian of the person of her minor child Tahsina Yasmin and directing her to hand over the custody of the said minor child to her father and ex-husband of the petitioner-appellant, Moabul Ahmed. 

 2. The petitioner-appellant Mrs. Nilufar Majid filed on 29-3-83 the aforesaid case in the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka u/s 25 of the said Act on the allegations, inter alia, that she was married to the opposite party-respondent Moqbul Ahmed on 11-7-76 and of the said wedlock a daughter named Tahsina Yasmin was born to them on 24-1-78. After the birth of the baby girl the respondent Moqbul Ahmed started to ill treat the appellant. He kicked her on her left eye on 7-11-79 and compelled her to leave her conjugal home with the child. She tried her best to go back to her husband for the ultimate Welfare of the minor girl but the respondent refused to take her and the baby girl back. As such the appellant was constrained to divorce the respondent Moqbul Ahmed on 27-11-80 after a year of separation and repeated attempts at reconciliation. The minor girl Tahsina Yasmin was all along in the custody of the appellant and the respondent Moqbul Ahmed never maintained or looked after her or visited her. The appellant was compelled to take up a job in a Bank in order to maintain her child. On 16-11-81 the appellant entered into a second marriage with P.W.2 Abdul Aziz Khan in order to provide a father-figure to the said minor who loves her new father very much. The second marriage was contracted after due deliberations to provide the child with, a complete family which, is essential for leer mental and physical development. The appellant is, entitled to become the guardian of the person; of the minor. As such the appellant prayed that she be appointed the guardian of the person of the said minor in terms of section 25 of the said Act. 

 3. The opposite party-respondent Moqbul Ahmed contested the case by filing a written objection. He admitted the marriage with the appellant but stated that the date of marriage was, 17-8,76 and not 11-7-76. He denied that-he ill-treated the appellant or kicked her on the left eye on 7-11-79 or, that the appellant was; forced to leave the conjugal home with the child or that he never maintained or visited the, child or that the child was always in the custody of the appellant. His case was that the minor child has been nursed, reared, and looked after, by the respondent with the best of love, care, affection and devotion since  her birth. The respondent has also given her motherly care. This was necessary as the appellant had a long been mentally unsound and callous to her duties both as a mother and as a wife. The child had been with her parents at the respondent's own house at 222/12A, Maghbazar, Dhaka since her birth. The respondent's further case is that, while living with him the appellant had led a dubious life the propensity of a society girl. She used to disregard the norms and sanctity of family life and left behind instances as a, faithless wife and irresponsible mother. Some ugly episodes of her philander came to the notice of the respondent and his relations. At this she suddenly deserted the conjugal home surreptitiously on 24-11-79 with the minor child while the respondent was away in his office. The appellant then started living with her elder brother, O.P.W.3 Abdul Hai at Dhanmondi. The respondent and his relations used to visit the child there and gave her maintenance including baby food, fruits, garments etc. respondent keenly awaited the return of the appellant to their conjugal home but instead she issued him a letter of divorce dated 27-11-80. The appellant, continued to live in the house of her brother O.P.W.3 Abdul Halim at Dhanmondi with the Child, after the said divorce. But, finding the child to be an impediment to her bohemian way of life she suddenly left. her brother's house keeping the child with her said brother O.P. W.3 Abdul Ham then gave the child back to the custody of the .respondent in June, 1981 and since then the respondent again started rearing the child with the same love, care and allocation as before, assisted by a host of his relations including his sister, brothers and their family. The child was admitted in 1982 to a prominent school of the city named "Maple Leaf International". She passed the Nursery class arid got portioned K.G. I in 1983. For all these periods the appellant did not care to enquire about the child. Suddenly in February, 1983 she paid a visit to the respondent's house to meet the child and then started visiting the respondent's house occasionally. On 25-3-83 she repeatedly requested the respondent over telephone to bring the child to her residence assuring that the child may be taken back just after a short visit. The respondent took the child to the appellant's residence which is a small flat, but the appellant slipped out of the house with the child by the back door. The respondent made frantic efforts for her recovery and ultimately lodged an F.I.R. with the Tejgaon Police on 28-3-83. This having been an abortive attempt he brought out a search warrant from the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and recovered the child from the appellant, but when the child was produced before the learned Magistrate on 5-4-83, the respondent was prevented from in taking the child into his custody as there was an order of ad-interim injunction issued by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in the present case which the appellant instituted an 29-3-83, after deceitfully taking away the child from him on 25-3-83. In the facts and circumstances of the case the respondent prayed that the appellant's application be dismissed. 

 5. Both the parties adduced evidence and submitted documents in support of their respective cases. The appellant examined 3 P.Ws. including herself as P.W.1. The respondent examined 3 O.P.Ws including himself as O.P.W.1. 

 7. Thereafter the appellant preferred this appeal. Before I advert to the merits of the appeal it is necessary to dispose of certain matters relating to the maintainability of the case itself. 

 8. The case was purportedly filed is 25 of the said Act. Section 25 of the said Act provides as follows: 

 9. The appellant did not set out a case in terms of section 25 of the said Act that the minor child was removed from the custody of a guardian of her person. Her application, therefore, was not maintainable 0:25 of the said Act. However, u/s 7 of the said Act any relation or friend of a minor ask for order of appointment of guardian of the person of a minor. This is actually what the appellant prayed for in the present case. Although section 25 was mentioned in the cause title, it was in substance an application under section 7 of the said Act. The application was also beard and disposed of in substantial compliance with the procedure provided in section 11 of the said Act. Under such circumstances the appellant's application can be treated as a proceeding u/s 7 of the said Act. 

 11." Earlier it has been noted that apart from filing a written objection in the case the respondent also filed on 12-5-83 an application u/s 25 of the said Act praying the appellant be directed to return the minor girl Tahsina Yasmin to the custody of the respondent who was all along the custodian of the said minor. The learned District Judge by order No. 9 dated 12-5-83 ordered that the said application be kept with the record for the present. While disposing of the case the learned District Judge treated the written objection filed by the respondent to be an application u/s 25 of the said Act. This was not necessary. The respondent had in fact filed a formal application u/s 25 of the said Act for disposal by the Court. The learned District Judge was probably unmindful of this application when he disposed of the case. He had full legal authority to pass an order concerning the custody of the child, as the respondent had already filed a formal application to that effect. The respondent need not have filed any application u/s 7 of the said Act because the father is the natural guardian of the minor child. 

 12. Coming now to the evidence adduced in this case P.W.1 Mrs. Nilufar Majid has stated her case as made out is the application. She stated in her examination-in-chief that she married for the second time for her own guardianship. She also stated that her present husband serves at Hotel Sonargaon while she serves in the Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd. She also stated that the respondent left the minor child with her on 25-3-83. The child reads at Maryland Kindergarten School. She stated that the child used to visit her brother's house from time to time and the respondent brought the child from her brother's house. The child never stayed at Maghbazar with her father. The mother of the appellant stayed in her house and her mother did not swear any affidavit. In cross-examination she denied the suggestion that she leads an in disciplined life and that she had never had the custody of the child. She also denied that she left for an unknown place with the child on 25-3-83 giving a false story of transfer to Chittagong. She also denied that she left the child to her elder brother's house and that her elder brother delivered the child to the respondent. She stated that she works in Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd. from 9 A.M. to 5 P.M. Her present, husband goes to office at 8-30 A.M. and comes back at 5. P.M. She also stated that during their absence the child stays with an Aya. She denied that she was treated for mental illness by Dr. Nizamuddowla. 

 15. As against the above evidence adduced by the appellant the respondent has deposed as O.P.W.1. He has stated his case as made out in the written objection. He has stated that he is an officer in the Bangladesh Bank. After his marriage with the appellant he found her to be bad tempered and of unsound mind. She was treated by Dr. Nimmuddowla who prescribed medicines for her. He submitted in the, prescription in Court. He stated that after the child was born he and his sister looked after the child. The appellant did not have any feeling for the child. Upto 25-3-83 the child was in his custody, After his marriage with the appellant the appellant used to get out of the house as soon as he went out to the office and at times she did not return in the night. She was seen to have roamed about with different persons. He and his elder sister forbade his wife not to go for such unrestrained mixing. The appellant left the conjugal home on 24-11-79 during his absence taking with her the child and some precious articles. She went to stay with her elder brother P.W.3 Abdul Hatim at Dhanmondi O.P.W.1 further narrated his case as made out in the written objection. He was cross-examined at length but it could not be established that he was making any untrue or exaggerated statement: O.P.W.2 Khodeja Akhtar is the mother of the appellant Mrs. Nilufar Majid. She stated in her examination-in-chief that her daughter ill-behaved with her husband. The appellant had no love and feeling for her child. The appellant left for the house of her eldest son with the child in November, 1979. The appellant told her en query that she left her husband's house because. She did not like her husband. Then the appellant left the house of her eldest son towards the middle of 1980 and no one knew where she went away. The appellant came to her (O.P.W.2) in December, 1980 and told her on query that she left the child in the house of her elder brother because the child cries. O.P.W.2 further stated that while the child was at the house or her eldest son, the father of the child used to visit the child and used to defray her expenses. She also stated that while her daughter was in her house her movement and behaviour were not restrained. She used to come back late at night and used to mix with men freely. She protested against it but the appellant did not pay any heed. The appellant also misbehaved with her. As she had done injuries to the family so by an affidavit dated 30-4-81 she severed all relationship with her daughter. She has filed the said affidavit in Court. She also stated that it would be better if the child of the appellant stays with the child's father. In cross-examination she stated that when the appellant came to the house of her eldest son she was there and she did not notice any mark of injury on her body. Various suggestions were given to this witness but there is no explanation as to why the mother should depose against her own daughter. 

 19. Before i discuss the evidence on record it is necessary to set up in brief the legal position with regard to the custody of a minor Muslim daughter. Under the Muslim Law the mother is entitled to the custody (hizanat) of her female child until she has attained puberty. The right continues though she is divorced by the father of the child, unless she marries a. second husband in which case the custody belongs to the father (Mulla—Principles of Muhammedan Law 15th Edn. section 352, page 291). It has been held in a number of cases, however, that though the mother loses her right to custody on the ground, of her re-marriage with a stranger, the Court has still to see whether in the interest of the welfare of the minor child the custody should remain with the mother. (Amer Ilahi V. Mst. Rashida Akhter, P.L.D. 1955 Lahore 412; Tumina Khtun V. Geharjan Bibi A.I.R. 1942 Calcutta 281; In re: Ghulam Muhammad Jaffar I.L.R. 1942 Kar. 363; Mst, Fatima and another V. Darwaz A.I.R. 1936 Pash. 63; Mst. Nazeer Begum and others V. Abdul Sattar P.L.D. 1963 Karachi 465. 

 20. It has been held by the learned District Judge in the present case that the second husband of the appellant P.W.2 Abdul Aziz Khan is a stranger and is not related to the minor child within the prohibited degrees. That finding of fact has not been challenged in this appeal. P.W.2 being a stranger the appellant has lost her traditional religious right of custody of the minor child. The mother can be given the custody of the child only if the Court is of opinion that the welfare of the minor child shall still be served best if the mother is given the custody. She cannot claim the custody of the minor child as a matter of right now. 

 22. Section 17 of the said Act is a clear pointer to the central consideration in appointing a guardian of a minor child. It is the welfare of the child which will be of paramount consideration. A mother who is married to a stranger loses her preferential right of custody over a minor child but that will not totally excluded her from being considered fit for guardianship if she is otherwise held on a consideration of all circumstances in a particular case to be competent to be the guardian of such minor. (Rahela Khatoon V. Ramele Khatoon 22 D.L.R. 245) 

 23. In forming an opinion as to whether even after re-marriage it would still be to the welfare of the minor child that she should remain tinder the guardianship, as well as the custody of the mother, facts and circumstances have to, be considered independently in each case. In the facts and circumstances of the present case it seems to me very clear indeed that the factual basis upon which the appellant has laid her claim on the guardianship of her minor child has not been established. It is only the appellant who as P.W. 1 has stated in evidence that, after the birth of the child the respondent used to beat her and ill-treat her. There is absolutely no corroborating evidence with regard to this .allegation. There is also no corroboration of the appellant's statement in evidence that on 7-11-79 the respondent has beaten both her and the child resulting in injuries to the body of the appellant. There is also no corroborating evidence that the child was all along with her and that the child was admitted to Maryland Kindergarten School. On the other hand she admits in her very examination-in-chief that the respondent took the minor child to the appellant on 25-3-83. Even her present husband P.W.2 Abdul Aziz Khan has not stated for how long the minor child is with them. P.W.2 married the appellant on 16-11-81 and he stated in, cross-examination that he does not know where the child stayed before his marriage. The appellant has failed to establish a consistent story that as the mother of the child it is she who reared her up from birth, gave her love and affection and in all respects cared for her all throughout. 

 25. Normally, when a daughter or a sister in the family goes astray the mother or the brother, as the case may be, tries to keep the matter within the family. In this case the mother and the brother of the appellant have gone to the extent of deposing in the Court against the conduct, character and way of life of the appellant in a manner which betrays a sense of despair and disgust on their part. No explanation can be found as to why the mother O.P.W.2 Khadija Akhtar deposed against her own daughter, unless her daughter's conduct was absolutely unbearable. A suggestion was made to her brother O.P.W.3 Abdul Halim that he wanted to deprive the appellant from her paternal properties, that he wanted to give the appellant in marriage with somebody also and that he wanted the guardianship of the minor child himself. The O.P.W.3 has denied these suggestions. No material has been placed in support of this suggestion and, therefore, these are suggestions for the sake of suggestions only without any basis. It has come out in bold relief in the evidence on record that the appellant's past life was not at all to the liking of her former husband, mother and brother and that she had never given the child the motherly care and affection she deserves. 

 29. Mr. Mohammadullah, learned Advocate for the respondent submits on the other hand that this plea of the appellant is in fact a feigned plea. The appellant has nothing but showmanship in all that she does. She has re-married just to show that she can re-marry. She played a trick on the respondent on 25-3-83 and took the custody of the child and thereafter filed this case on 29-3-83 only to show that she can get the custody and guardianship through Court. In paragraph 6 of the application in the present miscellaneous case the appellant stated that she married for the second time in order to provide a father-figure to the minor child who loves her new father very much. Mr. Mohammadullah submits that the very idea of having the guardianship of the minor child is to make the child forget about her real father and to train her to look upon P.W.2 as her real father. The object of filing this case is to deprive the respondent from his lawful right to rear up his child in the manner he thinks best. The appellant's object is to take away the child from her real father and to make her forget her real father. 

 30. In the facts and circumstances of the case I do not think that the submissions of Mr. Mohammadullah are far from correct. There is absolutely no material on record that the appellant has mended her ways and that the child would be brought up at her home in a manner congenial to the development of the child. There is a noticeable tendency on the part of the appellant to suppress facts. That the respondent was rearing up the child so long has been completely suppressed by her. She wants to say that her present husband loves the child very much and that he would be a father-figure to the child. The child, on the basis of the evidence on record, never lived with her present husband before 25-3-83. If her past conduct and way of life are a guide, it will be hazardous to make her the guardian of the person of the child. Mr. Huda submits that the present life-style of the appellant should be but the story of the appellant's neglect of the child is so recent that her present life offers no trust and confidence at all. 

 31. Finally it has been submitted that if this Court is disposed towards dismissing the appeal then the appellant may be given the right of visiting the minor child every day. I am not aware of any such arrangement in a case for guardianship. The order of the learned District Judge giving the appellant the right to visit the minor child twice a month at least seems to me to be a fair and reasonable order.
